\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:rh_intro}
% 2026-10-17 (user): prose rewritten in the style of Zhang, Zhang, Cucuringu, and Qian (2024).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Research question.} We investigate whether incorporating exogenous predictors improves intraday
  % 2026-10-17 (user, new-notes 1): parked -- the target is built from front-month E-mini futures (03_data, Realized moments). Was: "forecasts of the realized variance of the S\&P 500"
  forecasts of a futures-based (E-mini) proxy for the realized variance of the S\&P 500 over the closing half-hour interval.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Specifically, at the 15:30 ET forecast origin on trading day $t$, we seek to predict $\RV_t$, which
    denotes the realized variance over the 15:30--16:00 closing interval (see Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}).
  % 2026-10-22 (user): parked -- the pooled models are estimated on the 13 regular-hours bars (E34). Was: "Each intraday model is estimated across all $M = \rhdmNIntervals$ half-hour intervals of the trading day, and we evaluate its out-of-sample predictions on the forecast issued at 15:30 for the closing half hour."
  \item Each pooled intraday model is estimated on the \rhePoolNBars{} regular-hours half-hour bars of the trading
    day, and we evaluate its out-of-sample predictions on the forecast issued at 15:30 for the closing half hour.
  \item To isolate the contribution of the additional covariates, we compare the full predictor set against the
    HAR benchmark; the exogenous series constitute the exact difference between the two sets (see
    Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Motivation for the HAR baseline.} Following \citet{Corsi2009}, the standard HAR regression models
  realized volatility solely as a linear function of its own past lags. Consequently, it omits a rich set of
  exogenous variables available by 15:30, including higher-order realized moments, liquidity measures, the
  cross-section of constituent returns, news and social-media sentiment, option-implied volatility, volatility
  demand indicators, and scheduled macroeconomic and earnings announcements.
\item \textbf{Empirical design.} For each intraday interval $(t,i)$, we consider a single forecast mapping of
  the form
  \[
    \hat y_{t,i} = f_{m,\mathcal X,\mathcal I}(\bm x_{t,i}),
  \]
  indexed by the model class $m$ and the predictor set $\mathcal X \in \{\mathrm{HAR}, \mathrm{Full}\}$.
  % 2026-10-16 (user, E12): parked -- $\hat y_t = f_{m,\mathcal X,\mathcal I}(\bm x_t)$.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The primary empirical results reported in Section~\ref{sec:rh_results} focus on the pooled intraday
    estimation scheme, $\mathcal I = \{1, \dots, M\}$.
  % 2026-10-18 (user, new-notes 10): parked -- closing cadence only in the closing section. Was: "\item As our primary benchmark forecast, we employ the daily ordinary least squares (OLS) regression on the"
  \item As our primary benchmark forecast, we employ the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression on the
    % 2026-10-17 (user): parked -- closing-interval material (relabeled: closing-interval HAR benchmark). Was: "estimated exclusively on the closing interval (see"
    HAR benchmark predictor set, estimated exclusively on the closing interval (the closing-interval HAR benchmark; see
    Sections~\ref{sec:rh_methods_models} and~\ref{sec:rh_results_eval}).
  \item We evaluate predictive accuracy via the average QLIKE loss over the out-of-sample evaluation span
  % 2026-10-20 (user): parked -- Table 1 scored from 2012 (TABLE1_SWITCH.md, approved). Was: "$\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ from \rhoosSpanStart{} to \rhoosSpanEnd{} ($T_{\mathrm{oos}} = \rhoosDays$ trading days; see Section~\ref{sec:rh_results_eval})."
    $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ from \rhoosSpanStart{} to \rhoosSpanEnd{} ($T_{\mathrm{oos}} = \rhoosDays$
    % 2026-10-22 (user, E36): parked -- "the accuracy of the pooled linear models in Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}"; Table 1 now holds the tree ensembles too.
    trading days; see Section~\ref{sec:rh_results_eval}); the accuracy of the pooled linear models and tree
    ensembles in Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} is scored on every regular-hours bar from \rhorSpanStart{} to \rhorSpanEnd{}
    (\rhorDays{} trading days, a rolling window of \rhorWindowDays{} trading days).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Main findings.}
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-22 (user, E34: one design for the 12 pooled forecasts): parked -- "across every intraday model class" and "the elastic net achieves a statistically significant reduction" no longer hold with the pooled linear models on the trees' design (make_rehaul_results.py, E34 CLAIM); counts printed. Was: "\item Incorporating the full predictor set reduces the average out-of-sample QLIKE loss relative to the HAR benchmark across every intraday model class (\rhrAfPoolPairs{} classes in total, with \rhrAfPoolLowerSig{} of these reductions statistically significant at the 5\% level; see Section~\ref{sec:rh_results}). Among the linear specifications, the elastic net achieves a statistically significant reduction; among the tree ensembles, the reduction is statistically significant at the 5\% level in \rhrAfPoolTreeLowerSig{} of the three classes."
  \item Incorporating the full predictor set reduces the average out-of-sample QLIKE loss relative to the HAR
    benchmark in \rhrAfPoolLower{} of the \rhrAfPoolPairs{} intraday model classes, with \rhrAfPoolLowerSig{}
    of these reductions statistically significant at the 5\% level (see Section~\ref{sec:rh_results}).
    % 2026-10-22 (user, E34): parked -- with the base-5 pooled trees their reductions are no longer the largest or significant (make_rehaul_results.py, E34 CLAIM); no ranking. Was: "The tree-based ensembles exhibit the largest relative improvements, while among the linear specifications, the elastic net achieves a statistically significant reduction."
    The reduction is statistically significant at the 5\% level in \rhrAfPoolLinLowerSig{} of the three linear
    classes and in \rhrAfPoolTreeLowerSig{} of the three tree classes.
  % 2026-10-19 (user): parked -- the MSE finding, with the QLIKE/squared-error divergence bullet of 06_results.tex

  %   and none of the MSE differences is statistically significant.
  % 2026-10-17 (user): parked -- closing-interval material (relabeled: closing-interval HAR benchmark). Was: "than the closing-interval benchmark forecast."
  \item Every pooled intraday forecast incurs a higher average QLIKE loss than the closing-interval HAR
    % 2026-10-22 (user, E34): parked -- with the base-5 pooled trees the gap on the full predictor set is significant for \rhrVsBmPoolTreeFullSig{} of the three tree ensembles, not all (make_rehaul_results.py, E34 CLAIM). Was: "benchmark. While this performance gap is statistically insignificant at the 5\% level for the linear models, it is significant for the tree ensembles. Notably, augmenting the intraday models with the full predictor"
    % 2026-10-22 (user, E34: one design for the 12 pooled forecasts): parked -- "insignificant ... for the linear models" and "narrows this gap across all model classes" no longer hold (make_rehaul_results.py, E34 CLAIM); counts printed. Was: "benchmark. Under the full predictor set, this performance gap is statistically insignificant at the 5\% level for the linear models and significant for \rhrVsBmPoolTreeFullSig{} of the three tree ensembles. Notably, augmenting the intraday models with the full predictor set narrows this gap across all model classes (see Section~\ref{sec:rh_results_classes})."
    benchmark. Under the full predictor set, this performance gap is statistically significant at the 5\% level
    for \rhrVsBmPoolLinFullSig{} of the three linear models and for \rhrVsBmPoolTreeFullSig{} of the three tree
    ensembles. Augmenting the intraday models with the full predictor set narrows this gap in
    \rhrVsBmPoolNarrow{} of the \rhrAfPoolPairs{} model classes (see Section~\ref{sec:rh_results_classes}).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Economic application.} To assess the economic value of the forecasts on trading days with a
  % 2026-10-18 (user, second-list 20): parked -- SPXW is the weekly PM-settled series the strategy trades; SPX is the monthly. Was: "same-day SPX expiration"
  same-day SPXW expiration, we construct a trading strategy that takes a long or short position in a
  zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) at-the-money straddle based on the sign of the difference between the variance
  forecast and option-implied variance (see Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ}). Using the full predictor set increases
  the annualized Sharpe ratio of this strategy relative to the HAR benchmark in every intraday model class (see
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_results}).
% 2026-10-22 (user, E34: one design for the 12 pooled forecasts): parked -- the note named one class. % 2026-10-22 (user, D6): parked -- the note under the per-year ratio D1; under the Sharpe ratio of note D6 the sentence holds in point estimates. Was: "\editc{orange}{N15c}{Problem: ``every intraday model class'' does not hold: the full predictor set raises the pooled Sharpe ratio in \rhrAfPoolShHigher{} of the \rhrAfPoolPairs{} classes ($\Delta\SR$ from \rhrAfPoolDShMin{} to \rhrAfPoolDShMax); see note N15c in Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ}.}"
\editc{orange}{N15c}{Problem: under the Sharpe ratio of note D6, the full predictor set raises the pooled Sharpe ratio in \rhrAfPoolShHigher{} of the \rhrAfPoolPairs{} classes ($\Delta\SR$ from \rhrAfPoolDShMin{} to \rhrAfPoolDShMax), so ``every intraday model class'' holds in point estimates; \rhrAfPoolShHigherSig{} of these gains are statistically significant at the 5\% level (bootstrap test), and under the previous ratio the count was \rheDefDOnePos{} of \rheDefN{}. See notes N15c and D6 in Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ}.}
\item \textbf{Paper organization.} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_related} reviews the related literature. Section~\ref{sec:rh_data} describes the data and
  target construction, and Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors} details the benchmark and exogenous predictors.
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods} presents the forecasting models and rolling estimation protocol.
  % 2026-10-17 (user): parked -- closing-interval material (the variable-importance analysis covers the closing-interval models and is parked). Was: "reports the out-of-sample forecasting results and variable-importance analysis."
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_results} reports the out-of-sample forecasting results.
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ} evaluates the economic value of the forecasts in the 0DTE straddle strategy, and
  Section~\ref{sec:rh_conclusion} concludes.
\end{itemize}

%   $\E_t[\RV^{(1)}_{t+1}] = \beta_0 + \sum_{k} \beta_k\, \RV^{(k)}_t$, $k \in \{1,5,22\}$ trading days, with
%   $\RV^{(k)}_t$ the average daily realized variance over the last $k$ trading days. Our HAR components
%   $\bar y^{(k)}_t$ take the same averages of $y$ over $k$ intraday intervals.\newline
% 2026-10-15 (finish): parked -- the Introduction is parked, so Related work opens the paper; the bullet now defines
% E_t and the daily target and reads standalone. Was: "$\E_t[\RV_{t+1}] = \beta_0 + ...$, with $\RV^{(d)}_t$, ... the
% average daily realized variance over the last 1, 5 and 22 trading days. Our HAR components $\bar y^{(k)}_t$ take the
% same averages of $y$ over $k$ intraday intervals."
\item \textbf{Realized variance and the HAR model.} Following \citet{Corsi2009}, the heterogeneous
  autoregressive (HAR) model specifies the conditional expectation of next-day realized variance as a linear
  function of past realized variances aggregated over daily, weekly, and monthly horizons:
  $\E_t[\RV^{(d)}_{t+1}] = \beta_0 + \beta_d\, \RV^{(d)}_t + \beta_w\, \RV^{(w)}_t + \beta_m\, \RV^{(m)}_t$,
  where $\E_t$ denotes the conditional expectation given information available at the forecast origin on day $t$,
  and $\RV^{(d)}_t$, $\RV^{(w)}_t$, and $\RV^{(m)}_t$ denote the average daily realized variance over the
  preceding 1, 5, and 22 trading days, respectively. Because all three components represent daily realized
  variances aggregated at the daily, weekly, and monthly horizons, forecasting the realized variance of a
  specific intraday interval lies outside this standard daily specification.\newline
  See \citet{Corsi2009}, \citet{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003}, \citet{BarndorffNielsenShephard2004},
  \citet{AndersenBollerslevDiebold2007}, \citet{CorsiMittnikPigorschPigorsch2008},
  \citet{BollerslevPattonQuaedvlieg2016}, \citet{BekiermanManner2018}, \citet{BennedsenLundePakkanen2022},
  \citet{HansenHuangShek2012}, and \citet{AndersenBollerslevChristoffersenDiebold2006}.
  % 2026-10-16 (user, E1): parked -- Related work does not describe our estimators. The components, the square-root
  % target, and the 15:30 origin belong in Methods. Was: "... on day $t$ (here 15:30 ET) and ... Our HAR components
  % $\bar y^{(k)}_t$ take the same averages over $k$ intraday intervals of $y$, the square root of realized variance
  % divided by its diurnal adjustment (Section~\ref{sec:rh_data})."
  % \editc{red}{E1}{Related work says the HAR components average $y$... Predictors and Methods average $\tilde y$.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item In a multivariate setting, the panel HAR framework of \citet{BollerslevHoodHussLebedev2018} estimates a
    single pooled regression jointly across a cross-section of assets.
    % 2026-10-16 (user, E1): parked -- this named our estimator. Was: "the cross-asset counterpart of our intraday
    % model, which pools the intraday intervals of one index."
    % Key says "Lebedev"; the bib's author field (correctly) says Pedersen -- \citet prints the author field.
  \item For the theoretical foundations of realized variance, see \citet{BarndorffNielsenShephard2002}.
  % 2026-10-15 (bib pass): parked -- the [to add] placeholder, now a \citet key in references.bib. Was:
  % \item \todo{to add: Barndorff-Nielsen--Shephard 2002 (realized variance)}.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Diurnal pattern.} It is well documented that intraday return volatility exhibits a pronounced
  U-shaped pattern across the trading session. To account for this periodicity, standard practice scales intraday
  realized variance by a diurnal factor estimated from the corresponding clock-time interval on prior trading
  days.\newline
  % 2026-10-16 (user, E1): parked -- the display was our target, not the literature's. Was:
  % "divides by a diurnal adjustment, here $y_{t,i} = \sqrt{\RV_{t,i}/s^2_{t,i}}$, with $\RV_{t,i}$ the realized
  % variance of intraday interval $i$ on day $t$ and $s^2_{t,i}$ its diurnal adjustment."
  See \citet{AndersenBollerslev1997} on intraday periodicity, \citet{EngleGallo2006} on intraday range and
  volatility measures as indicators of daily volatility, and \citet{HizmeriBevilacqua2025} on morning
  volatility uncertainty.
  % 2026-10-15 (notation pass): EngleGallo2006 is a multiple-indicators model of daily volatility, not a periodicity
  % paper; its claim is narrowed to what it shows.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item See also \citet{TaylorXu1997} on diurnal volatility adjustments and \citet{EngleSokalska2012} on
    multiplicative decompositions of intraday volatility.
  % 2026-10-15 (bib pass): parked -- the [to add] placeholder, now \citet keys in references.bib. Was:
  % \item \todo{to add: Taylor--Xu 1997 (periodicity factor); Engle--Sokalska 2012 (intraday volatility)}.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{0DTE options and the variance risk premium.} The variance risk premium, defined as the difference
  between option-implied variance and expected realized variance,
  $\E^{\mathbb{Q}}_t[\RV_t] - \E^{\mathbb{P}}_t[\RV_t]$, under the risk-neutral ($\mathbb Q$) and physical
  ($\mathbb P$) measures (where $\RV_t$ denotes the realized variance through expiration), is empirically
  positive on average.\newline
  See \citet{HizmeriBevilacqua2025}, as well as the foundational option-pricing frameworks of
  \citet{BlackScholes1973} and \citet{Merton1973}.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item On zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) options, see \citet{BandiFusariReno2023},
    \citet{BeckmeyerBrangerGayda2023}, \citet{BrogaardHanWon2023}, \citet{DimErakerVilkov2024},
    \citet{Vilkov2026}, and \citet{AlmeidaFreireHizmeri2025}; on the variance risk premium more broadly, see
    \citet{CarrWu2009} and \citet{BollerslevTauchenZhou2009}.
  % 2026-10-15 (bib pass): parked -- the [to add] placeholder, now \citet keys in references.bib. Was:
  % \item \todo{to add: Bandi--Fusari--Ren\`o 2023; Beckmeyer--Branger--Gayda 2023; Brogaard--Han--Won 2023;
  %   Dim--Eraker--Vilkov 2024; Vilkov, 0DTE trading rules; Almeida--Freire--Hizmeri 2025; Carr--Wu 2009;
  %   Bollerslev--Tauchen--Zhou 2009}.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Machine learning for volatility and returns.} A growing literature models conditional return and
  volatility dynamics via flexible nonlinear mappings $f(\bm x_t)$ of a high-dimensional predictor vector
  $\bm x_t$.\newline
  See \citet{gu2020empirical} for return prediction and \citet{christensen2023machine} for realized volatility
  forecasting; for gradient-boosted decision trees, see \citet{Ke2017} (LightGBM) and \citet{Chen2016}
  (XGBoost); for Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, see \citet{Akiba2019} (Optuna).
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- NN content parked for now. Was: "...; realized volatility: \citet{Bucci2020},
  % \citet{RahimikiaPoon2020}, \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}; MinGRU \citet{Feng2024}; PufferLib \citet{Suarez2024}."
  \item For ensemble methods, see \citet{Breiman2001} on random forests and \citet{Friedman2001} on gradient
    boosting; for machine-learning applications to realized volatility and intraday commonality, see
    \citet{Bucci2020}, \citet{RahimikiaPoon2020}, and \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}.
  % 2026-10-15 (bib pass): parked -- the [to add] placeholder, now \citet keys in references.bib. Was:
  % \item \todo{to add: Breiman 2001; Friedman 2001 (gradient boosting); Bucci 2020; Rahimikia--Poon 2020;
  %   Zhang--Zhang--Cucuringu--Qian 2024; MinGRU (Feng et al.\ 2024); PufferLib}.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-16 (user): parked -- forecast evaluation is standard. Cite Patton, Diebold--Mariano,
% Harvey--Leybourne--Newbold, Newey--West, Ehm, and the model-confidence set where those methods are used
% (Forecast evaluation, Statistical tests, Economic value). Mincer--Zarnowitz and White's reality check are not used.
% \item \textbf{Forecast evaluation:} QLIKE is robust to noise in the volatility proxy: with a conditionally unbiased
%   proxy it ranks forecasts as the true conditional variance would, and
%   $\argmin_{v > 0} \E_t[\QLIKE(\RV_t, v)] = \E_t[\RV_t]$, with
%   $\QLIKE(\RV, v) = \RV/v - \log(\RV/v) - 1$.\newline
%   \citet{Patton2011} (robust loss functions), \citet{DieboldMariano1995} with the small-sample correction of
%   \citet{HarveyLeybourneNewbold1997}, \citet{HansenLundeNason2011} (model confidence set), \citet{Ehm2016}
%   (Murphy diagrams, elementary scores), \citet{MincerZarnowitz1969} (forecast-efficiency regressions).
%   \begin{itemize}
%   \item \citet{Hansen2005} (superior predictive ability), \citet{White2000} (reality check), \citet{RomanoWolf2005}
%     (StepM), \citet{NeweyWest1987} (HAC variance).
%   % 2026-10-15 (bib pass): parked -- the [to add] placeholder, now \citet keys in references.bib. Was:
%   % \item \todo{to add: Hansen 2005 (superior predictive ability); White 2000 (reality check); Romano--Wolf 2005
%   %   (StepM); Newey--West 1987 (HAC variance)}.
%   \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Shrinkage with many weak signals.} In high-dimensional linear regressions, penalized estimators
  regularize the coefficient vector via
  \[
    \hat{\bm\beta} = \argmin_{\bm\beta} \lVert \bm y - \bm X\bm\beta \rVert_2^2
      + \lambda\bigl(\alpha \lVert\bm\beta\rVert_1 + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2} \lVert\bm\beta\rVert_2^2\bigr)
  \]
  for a response vector $\bm y$, a predictor matrix $\bm X$, and an overall penalty strength $\lambda$, nesting
  ridge regression ($\alpha = 0$) and the lasso ($\alpha = 1$) as special cases; multi-penalty ridge extensions
  assign distinct regularization weights across feature blocks via $\lambda \sum_j \omega_j \beta_j^2$, where the
  penalty weight $\omega_j$ is held constant within each block.\newline
  See \citet{GiannoneLenzaPrimiceri2021} on dense versus sparse representations, \citet{ShenXiu2025} on
  learning from many weak signals, \citet{KozakNagelSantosh2020} on shrinking the cross-section of returns,
  \citet{HoerlKennard1970} on ridge regression, \citet{Tibshirani1996} on the lasso, \citet{ZouHastie2005} on the
  elastic net, and \citet{vandeWiel2021multipenalty} and \citet{vanWieringen2023ridge} on multi-penalty ridge
  estimation.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item See also \citet{Zou2006} on the adaptive lasso and feature-specific penalty weights, and
    \citet{FriedmanHastieTibshirani2010} on coordinate-descent estimation under the elastic-net
    parametrization.
  % 2026-10-15 (bib pass): parked -- the [to add] placeholder, now \citet keys in references.bib. Was:
  % \item \todo{to add: Zou 2006 (adaptive lasso, penalty weights); Friedman--Hastie--Tibshirani 2010 (elastic-net
  %   parametrization)}.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-16 (user): parked -- SHAP is standard. The decomposition and the Lundberg cites stay in Variable
% importance, where the values are computed. Aas et al. (dependent features) is not used.
% \item \textbf{Variable importance:} Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) decompose each forecast additively,
%   $\hat y_t = \phi_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_{t,j}$, with $\phi_{t,j}$ the contribution of predictor $j$ of $p$ and
%   $\phi_0$ the average forecast.\newline
%   \citet{lundberg2017unified} (SHAP), \citet{lundberg2018consistent} (TreeSHAP), \citet{aas2021explaining}
%   (dependent features).
% 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- no smearing mentions
% \item \textbf{Retransformation} (one sentence): a smearing estimate would correct $\hat y_t^{\,2} s^2_{t,c}$ for
%   retransformation bias; we do not.\newline
%   \citet{Duan1983}, \citet{ManningMullahy2001}.
\end{itemize}

\section{Data}
\label{sec:rh_data}
% 2026-10-17 (user): prose rewritten in the style of Zhang, Zhang, Cucuringu, and Qian (2024).
\begin{itemize}
% 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- "park all tables that I haven't mentioned in this chat". Was: \item \textbf{Sources} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_sources}).
\item \textbf{Data sources.}
  We group the exogenous covariates into eight distinct categories.
  % 2026-10-17 (user): parked -- closing-interval material (moved to Appendix app:rh_closing_sample). Was: "Specifically, the closing-interval specifications incorporate all \rhfiNExog{} exogenous series, whereas the pooled intraday specifications employ the"
  % 2026-10-19 (user): parked -- the pooled model includes the FOMC series (author decision). Was: "Specifically, the pooled intraday specifications employ the \rhdmNSeriesPooled{} series across all categories except the FOMC group."
  Specifically, the pooled intraday specifications employ
  the \rhdmNSeriesPooled{} series across all categories, the FOMC group included. A complete list and definition of
  each individual series is provided in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:rh_dm_dictionary}.
  % 2026-10-17 (user, E5/E2): bucket wording from data_explainer_v11 (front month, one-minute log-price
  % change, constituent 5-minute moments, turnover, spreads, StockTwits, volatility demand). The vendor,
  % the price print, and the bin list stay open in note E2.
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-17 (user, E5): parked -- the source list before the bucket exposition. Was:
  % \item \textbf{E-mini S\&P 500 futures (ES),} nearly 24 hours a day, 1998--2024, sampled on a 30-minute grid.
  %   Trading day $t = 1, \dots, T$; intraday interval $i = 1, \dots, M$, the half-hour intervals of the day; the
  %   closing interval $i = c$ is the closing half hour (15:30--16:00 ET).
  % \item $r_{t,i,k}$: the $k$-th one-minute log return in interval $i$ of day $t$, $k = 1, \dots, N_{t,i}$, with
  %   $N_{t,i} \le 30$.
  \item \textbf{Realized moments} (\bkSizeMom{} series). We obtain intraday data on the front-month E-mini
    S\&P 500 futures contract (defined as the most actively traded contract), which trades nearly 24 hours a day
    from 1998 through 2024, aggregated onto a 30-minute grid. Here, $t = 1, \dots, T$ indexes trading days and
    $i = 1, \dots, M$ indexes the half-hour intervals within day $t$, each ending on a half-hour timestamp; in
    particular, $i = c$ denotes the 15:30--16:00 ET closing interval. Each realized moment for interval $(t,i)$
    is computed by summing the corresponding one-minute quantity across all non-missing minutes within that half
    hour.
  \item Let $r_{t,i,k}$ denote the one-minute log-price change of the front-month contract for the $k$-th
    non-missing minute in interval $i$ of day $t$, where $k = 1, \dots, N_{t,i}$ and $N_{t,i} \le 30$.
    Following \citet{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003}, we define the realized variance over interval $(t,i)$
    as
    \[
      \RV_{t,i} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{t,i}} r_{t,i,k}^2 .
    \]
  \item We construct the \bkSizeMom{} exogenous realized-moment series as analogous one-minute sums over interval
    $(t,i)$ (note that $\RV_{t,i}$ above serves as our forecast target and is not counted among the exogenous
    series):
    % 2026-10-19 (user): raw parquet names for now (\ifrawseries, paper_rehaul.tex preamble): each sum is named by its
    % column of data/core_stats.parquet. The \else branch is the display of the symbols, unchanged.
    \ifrawseries
    \begin{gather*}
      \sername{sumret}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}, \quad \sername{sumabsret}_{t,i} = \sum_k |r_{t,i,k}|, \quad
      \sername{sumret3}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^3,\\
      \sername{sumret4}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^4, \quad
      \sername{sumpret2}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^2\,\mathbf{1}\{r_{t,i,k} > 0\},\\
      \sername{sumbipow}_{t,i} = \sum_{k \ge 2} |r_{t,i,k}|\,|r_{t,i,k-1}|, \quad
      \sername{sumautocov}_{t,i} = \sum_{k \ge 2} r_{t,i,k}\, r_{t,i,k-1}.
    \end{gather*}
    \else
    \[
      \sum_k r_{t,i,k}, \quad \sum_k |r_{t,i,k}|, \quad \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^3, \quad \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^4, \quad
      \mathrm{RS}^{+}_{t,i} = \sum_k r_{t,i,k}^2\,\mathbf{1}\{r_{t,i,k} > 0\},
    \]
    \[
      \mathrm{BV}_{t,i} = \sum_{k \ge 2} |r_{t,i,k}|\,|r_{t,i,k-1}|, \qquad
      \mathrm{AC}_{t,i} = \sum_{k \ge 2} r_{t,i,k}\, r_{t,i,k-1}.
    \]
    \fi
    % 2026-10-18 (user, second-list 14): parked -- quarticity normalization matched to the Table 5 note and RQ row (unscaled, without N/3); "prior to dividing by RV^2/N" dropped. Was: "Specifically, the third and fourth sums correspond to the unnormalized realized skewness and realized quarticity of \citet{AmayaChristoffersenJacobsVasquez2015} (that is, prior to dividing by $\RV^{3/2}_{t,i}/\sqrt{N_{t,i}}$ and $\RV^{2}_{t,i}/N_{t,i}$, respectively). Furthermore,"
    Specifically, the third sum corresponds to the unnormalized realized skewness of
    \citet{AmayaChristoffersenJacobsVasquez2015} (that is, prior to dividing by $\RV^{3/2}_{t,i}/\sqrt{N_{t,i}}$), and
    the fourth sum is the unscaled realized quarticity (without the factor $N_{t,i}/3$). Furthermore,
    % 2026-10-19 (user): series names through \ser (raw names for now). Was: "$\mathrm{RS}^{+}_{t,i}$",
    % "$\mathrm{BV}_{t,i}$", "$\mathrm{AC}_{t,i}$"
    $\ser{sumpret2}{\mathrm{RS}^{+}}_{t,i}$ denotes the positive realized semivariance of
    \citet{BarndorffNielsenKinnebrockShephard2010}, $\ser{sumbipow}{\mathrm{BV}}_{t,i}$ denotes the unscaled bipower variation
    of \citet{BarndorffNielsenShephard2004} (without the $\pi/2$ normalization factor), and $\ser{sumautocov}{\mathrm{AC}}_{t,i}$
    denotes the first-order realized autocovariance.
    % Sums read off the column names: the builder of data/core_stats.parquet is not in the repo
    % (live/close_signal/features.py:1-25). sumpret2 = positive semivariance is an assumed reading; bipower is
    % unnormalised (no pi/2). numobs is described three ways (outline flag 12; loading.py:349 calls it a tick count).
  % 2026-10-17 (user, E5): parked -- the one-line constituent list. The liquidity and market bullets replace it.
  % Was: Cross-section of index constituents, equal- and value-weighted (EW, VW), 1993--2024: six return
  % moments, turnover, order-flow imbalance (signed turnover) and bid-ask spreads.
  \item \textbf{Liquidity} (\bkSizeLiq{} series). From the front-month futures contract, we include total contract
    % 2026-10-19 (user): raw names for now; $N_{t,i}$ stays the count in the formulas above, the series is named after it.
    volume traded during the half hour as well as the number of observed one-minute intervals
    $N_{t,i}$\ifrawseries{} (\sername{numobs})\fi. In
    addition, using intraday data on S\&P 500 constituents from 1993 to 2024, we construct both equal-weighted
    and value-weighted cross-sectional aggregates of share turnover, buyer-initiated turnover, seller-initiated
    turnover, the effective spread, the quoted spread, and order-flow imbalance. Here, constituent turnover is
    defined as the number of shares traded during the half hour divided by prior-day shares outstanding, while
    buyer- and seller-initiated turnover aggregate trades according to their estimated trade direction. The
    effective spread measures the average percentage deviation between the transaction price and the prevailing
    mid-quote, and the quoted spread measures the average percentage bid--ask spread. Equal-weighted aggregates
    take simple cross-sectional averages across constituents, whereas value-weighted aggregates weight each
    % 2026-10-19 (user): series names through \ser (raw names for now). Was: "($\mathrm{OFI}^{\mathrm{EW}}$ and
    % $\mathrm{OFI}^{\mathrm{VW}}$)". The generic $\mathrm{OFI}_{t,i}$ of the display stays: it defines both.
    constituent by its prior-day market capitalization. For each weighting scheme ($\ser{ofi_ewstock}{\mathrm{OFI}^{\mathrm{EW}}}$
    and $\ser{ofi_vwstock}{\mathrm{OFI}^{\mathrm{VW}}}$), we define order-flow imbalance as
    \[
      \mathrm{OFI}_{t,i} = \frac{\mathrm{Buy}_{t,i} - \mathrm{Sell}_{t,i}}{\mathrm{Buy}_{t,i} + \mathrm{Sell}_{t,i}}
        \in [-1, 1],
      \qquad \text{missing if } \mathrm{Buy}_{t,i} + \mathrm{Sell}_{t,i} = 0 ,
    \]
    where $\mathrm{Buy}_{t,i}$ and $\mathrm{Sell}_{t,i}$ denote the aggregate buyer- and seller-initiated
    turnover in interval $i$ of day $t$, respectively.
    % loading.py:161-180, built on the unfilled legs.
  % 2026-10-17 (user, E5): parked -- one line per remaining group. The bullets below replace them.
  % Was: StockTwits attention and sentiment measures, from 2009 and 2010.
  % Was: Cboe volatility indices: VIX (from 2006), VIX3M (from 2009) and VVIX (from 2012), all to February 2024.
  % Was: Cboe option-volume series (the volatility-demand group), 2011 to August 2023.
  % Was: FOMC announcement times, 1993 to November 2023.
  \item \textbf{Equal-weighted market} (\bkSizeMew{} series) and \textbf{value-weighted market} (\bkSizeMvw{}
    series). For each weighting scheme described above, we compute six cross-sectional constituent return
    moments: realized variance, realized skewness, realized quarticity, absolute variation, bipower variation,
    and positive semivariance. In contrast to the futures moments, which are constructed from one-minute
    log-price changes, these constituent moments are computed from 5-minute log returns. Moreover, the
    constituent moment groups omit signed returns and realized autocovariance, whereas the exogenous futures
    moment group omits realized variance (which serves as the target variable).
  \item \textbf{Sentiment} (\bkSizeSent{} series). Using StockTwits message streams beginning in 2009 for total
    posts and 2010 for user-tagged posts, we construct three half-hourly indicators: investor attention, defined
    as the total number of posts within the half hour; a sentiment score that equals $1$ when all tagged posts
    are bullish and $-1$ when all tagged posts are bearish; and the sentiment count, defined as the number of
    posts carrying either a bullish or bearish tag.
  \editc{orange}{E30}{Decision: open, for the professor.\\Problem: the text gives only the $\pm 1$ endpoints of the sentiment score.\\
Question for the professor: what is the formula of the score between the endpoints, and what value does it take on intervals with no tagged posts? The repository receives the score precomputed (data/spy\_and\_sentiment.parquet, column stocktwits\_sentiment, first observed in June 2010); src/data/loading.py:280 reads it as a net score in $[-1, 1]$, and no script in src/ or experiments/ computes it.}
  \item \textbf{Implied volatility} (\bkSizeIv{} series). We include three Cboe volatility indices: the 30-day
    S\&P 500 implied volatility index (VIX, available from 2006), the three-month implied volatility index
    (VIX3M, from 2009), and the implied volatility of the VIX (VVIX, from 2012), all extending through February
    2024.
  \item \textbf{Volatility demand} (\bkSizeVd{} series). Using Cboe option-volume records from 2011 through
    August 2023, we measure net vega purchased by non-market-maker participants across four series formed by
    crossing two option universes—options on the S\&P 500 index and top S\&P 500 exchange-traded funds versus

\section{Methods}
\label{sec:rh_methods}
\subsection{Problem formulation}
\label{sec:rh_methods_setup}
\begin{itemize}
% 2026-10-15 (notation pass): parked -- code jargon replaced by the standard description below.
% \item \textbf{Time-series regression,} run as a causal walk-forward backtest; every input known at 15:30.
% 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- "re-estimated daily" -> "re-estimated every period" (two training schemes,
% Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_schemes}). Was: "\textbf{Rolling-window out-of-sample exercise,} re-estimated daily;

Was: "A period corresponds to a 30-minute intraday interval under our pooled intraday scheme (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_schemes}) and to a trading day for the daily benchmark forecast (Section~\ref{sec:rh_results_eval})."
\item \textbf{Rolling-window out-of-sample exercise.} We conduct a rolling-window out-of-sample forecasting exercise in which each model is re-estimated every period using only predictors in the information set $\mathcal F_t$ available at the 15:30 ET forecast origin. A period corresponds to a 30-minute intraday interval under our pooled intraday scheme (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_schemes}).
\item \textbf{Notation.} We index trading days by $t = 1, \dots, T$ and the 30-minute intraday intervals of day $t$ (including the overnight session) by $i = 1, \dots, M$, where $i = c$ denotes the closing half-hour interval (15:30--16:00 ET).
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-16 (formula pass): parked -- RV_{t,i} = sum_k r_{t,i,k}^2 and the lag (t, i-j) are defined once
  % in Data (sec:rh_data). Was: the sum, with r_{t,i,k} the kth one-minute log return and N_{t,i} <= 30
  % (Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold and Labys 2003); and "(t, i-j): the jth retained interval before (t,i)".
  \item Realized variance $\RV_{t,i}$ and the lag operator $(t, i-j)$ are defined in Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}. Our primary forecast target is the realized variance of the closing interval, $\RV_t \equiv \RV_{t,c}$.
  \item We denote by $\mathcal F_t$ the information set containing all data observed through 15:30 ET on day $t$, and write $\E_t[\cdot] \equiv \E[\,\cdot \mid \mathcal F_t]$ and $\Var_t(\cdot) \equiv \Var(\,\cdot \mid \mathcal F_t)$ for the corresponding conditional expectation and variance.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- the window lengths 20 and 5 are implementation; they move to Experimental setup
% (sec:rh_exp_samples) as n_d and \underline n_d. Was:
% \mathcal D_{t,i} = \{\text{last } 20 \text{ trading days } t' < t \text{ with interval } i\}, \qquad
% |\mathcal D_{t,i}| \ge 5 . ... \item Intervals with $|\mathcal D_{t,i}| < 5$: not scored.
\item \textbf{Diurnal adjustment.} Following \citet{AndersenBollerslev1997}, we remove the intraday diurnal pattern using the trailing sample mean of realized variance in the same time-of-day interval strictly prior to day $t$:
  \begin{gather*}
    s^2_{t,i} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal D_{t,i}|}\sum_{t' \in \mathcal D_{t,i}} \RV_{t',i}, \\
    \mathcal D_{t,i} = \{\text{last } n_{\mathrm{d}} \text{ trading days } t' < t \text{ with interval } i\}, \qquad
    |\mathcal D_{t,i}| \ge \underline n_{\mathrm{d}} .
  \end{gather*}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item For intervals with $|\mathcal D_{t,i}| < \underline n_{\mathrm{d}}$, we set $s^2_{t,i} = 1$ and exclude the interval from evaluation. The window parameters $n_{\mathrm{d}}$ and $\underline n_{\mathrm{d}}$ are given in Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_samples}.
  \end{itemize}
  % src/features/transforms/target.py:24-25, 286-298 (per slot rolling(20, min_periods=5).mean().shift(1); no
  % per-slot band on the target).
% 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- the window 240 and the levels 1/99 are implementation; they move to Experimental setup

% 240\}, \tilde y_{t,i} = \clip(y_{t,i}, Q_{0.01}(\mathcal Y_{t,i}), Q_{0.99}(\mathcal Y_{t,i}))"; "\item $Q_{0.01}(\cdot)$,
% $Q_{0.99}(\cdot)$: empirical 1st and 99th percentiles; $\clip$ truncates ..."; "\item Bounds: rolling quantiles of
% the previous 240 intervals, all intervals of the day pooled."
\item \textbf{Regression target.} To stabilize the variance, we take the square root of the diurnally adjusted realized variance and winsorize the resulting series at rolling lower and upper empirical quantiles:
  \begin{gather*}
    y_{t,i} = \sqrt{\RV_{t,i} / s^2_{t,i}}, \qquad
    \mathcal Y_{t,i} = \{y_{t,i-j} : j = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{w}}\}, \\
    \tilde y_{t,i} = \clip\bigl(y_{t,i},\; \underline Q_{t,i},\; \overline Q_{t,i}\bigr).
  \end{gather*}
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-15 (consolidation): parked -- the generic level p clashes with the number of predictors p.

The quantile levels and window length $n_{\mathrm{w}}$ are reported in Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_samples}.

  \item For the scored interval $i = c$ (the closing half hour that every model forecasts), we write $y_t \equiv y_{t,c}$ and
    $\tilde y_t \equiv \tilde y_{t,c}$.

\item \textbf{Back-transformation.} To obtain a variance forecast in raw units, we square the fitted volatility and multiply by the diurnal factor without post-estimation recalibration:
  \[
    \hat\sigma^2_t = \hat y_t^{\,2}\, s^2_{t,c},

  where $\hat y_t \equiv \hat y_{t,c}$ is the forecast of the winsorized target $\tilde y_t$, not of the unclipped $y_t$, formed using $\mathcal F_t$.
% 2026-10-17 (user, E10): parked -- decision applied (the sentence above now names \tilde y_t). Was:
% \editc{red}{E10}{Decision: say $\hat y_t$ forecasts $\tilde y_t$.\\Problem: the fit minimizes squared error in the clipped target $\tilde y$, and the back-transform sentence calls $\hat y_t$ a forecast of the unclipped $y_t$. QLIKE is then scored on the unwinsorized $\RV_{t,c}$.\\
% $y_t$, defined as $y_{t,c}$, is the square root of realized variance on the closing interval before any clipping. $\tilde y_t$ is that square root after the rolling 1st and 99th percentiles have pulled the tails in, and the estimation objective chooses $\hat y$ by minimizing squared error in $\tilde y$, not in $y$. The back-transform undoes the diurnal adjustment by squaring the fitted value, $\hat\sigma^2_t=\hat y_t^2 s^2_{t,c}$, and it sets $\hat y_t$ equal to the closing-interval fit $\hat y_{t,c}$. The sentence under the display then calls $\hat y_t$ a forecast of $y_t$. The loss that is scored, QLIKE, is computed from the unwinsorized $\RV_{t,c}$. The number that comes out of the regression is a fitted value for the clipped series. The sentence describes the square of that fitted value as a forecast of the unclipped series.}
  \begin{itemize}
% 2026-10-17 (user, new-notes 12): parked -- the calibration diagnostics are not reported (note E33). Was: "that we leave uncorrected and report explicitly in our calibration diagnostics."
  \item Because $\E_t[y_t^2] - (\E_t[y_t])^2 = \Var_t(y_t) \ge 0$, squaring the level forecast introduces a downward Jensen inequality bias that we leave uncorrected (note E33).
  \end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Rolling estimation window.} Under the intraday scheme, the estimation window at origin $(t,i)$ is $\mathcal W_{t,i}$ (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_schemes}), consisting of the $W$ most recent intervals prior to $(t,i)$. We let $\mathcal I$ denote the subset of intraday intervals included in estimation.

  %   \begin{itemize}

  %     $W = \cmPtFitWin$ trading days; re-estimated daily.
  %   \item Pooled intraday model ($\mathcal I = \{1, \dots, M\}$): all $M = 48$ intervals; $W = 24{,}000$ intervals,
  %     $\mathcal W_{t,i} = \{(t, i-W), \dots, (t, i-1)\}$; re-estimated every interval (trees).

\item \textbf{Hyperparameter-selection splits.} In line with \citet{gu2020empirical}, we partition the rolling window forward in time into an estimation subsample, an embargo gap of $n_{\mathrm{gap}}$ observations, and a validation subsample of $n_{\mathrm{val}}$ observations:
  \begin{gather*}
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{est}}_{t,i} = \{(t,\, i - W), \dots, (t,\, i - n_{\mathrm{val}} - n_{\mathrm{gap}} - 1)\}, \\
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t,i} = \{(t,\, i - n_{\mathrm{val}} - n_{\mathrm{gap}}), \dots,
      (t,\, i - n_{\mathrm{val}} - 1)\}, \\
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{val}}_{t,i} = \{(t,\, i - n_{\mathrm{val}}), \dots, (t,\, i - 1)\}.
  \end{gather*}
  Target interval $(t,i)$ never enters any of these sets. The lengths $n_{\mathrm{gap}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{val}}$ are given in Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_samples}.

% block), but the forecast at origin t is estimated on the full window W_t (ridge / elastic net below; the
% network's refit). W^est_t applies when hyperparameters are selected.
\item \textbf{Estimation objective.} Each model is estimated by minimizing the sum of squared errors on the scale of $\tilde y$. At forecast origin $(t,i)$, the parameter vector $\bm\theta$ is fitted over the full rolling window $\mathcal W_{t,i}$:
  \[
    \hat{\bm\theta}_{t,i} = \argmin_{\bm\theta} \sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal W_{t,i}}
      \bigl(\tilde y_{t',i'} - \hat y_{t',i'}(\bm\theta)\bigr)^2 .
  \]
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Here $(t',i')$ indexes the historical intervals in the window $\mathcal W_{t,i}$, and $\bm\theta$ collects the model parameters.
  \item During hyperparameter tuning only, candidate configurations are estimated on $\mathcal W^{\mathrm{est}}_{t,i}$ rather than $\mathcal W_{t,i}$ and evaluated on $\mathcal W^{\mathrm{val}}_{t,i}$.

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Models}
\label{sec:rh_methods_models}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{HAR and the HAR benchmark via OLS.} Following \citet{Corsi2009}, we specify the linear heterogeneous autoregressive model for each intraday interval $(t,i)$ as
  % 2026-10-16 (formula pass): parked -- the average and the horizon set are defined once in Predictors.

  \]
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The horizon set $\mathcal K$ and the lagged volatility averages $\bar y^{(k)}_{t,i}$ are defined in Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}, where $\bar y^{(k)}_{t,i}$ is the mean of the winsorized target over the $k$ half-hour intervals preceding $(t,i)$, including overnight intervals. The scored forecast is the closing-interval prediction $\hat y_t \equiv \hat y_{t,c}$.
  % 2026-10-16 (user, E12): parked -- the display had no interval index, so it was the closing-interval equation.
  % Was: $\hat y_t = \beta_0 + \sum_{k \in \mathcal K} \beta^{(k)}\, \bar y^{(k)}_t + \bm\delta^{\top} \bm D_t$,

  \item \textbf{Gradient boosting} \citep{Friedman2001}, implemented via LightGBM \citep{Ke2017} and XGBoost \citep{Chen2016}, minimizes the squared-error loss $\tfrac12 (\tilde y - F)^2$ over boosting rounds $b = 1, \dots, B$ with learning rate $\eta$. Each regression tree $f_b$ partitions the predictor space into $J$ leaves with leaf weights $\bm w$, where leaf $j$ contains the observation subset $\mathcal R_j$ of size $n_j = |\mathcal R_j|$. When the $\ell_1$ leaf penalty $\lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}} = 0$, the additive update and optimal leaf weight take the form
    \begin{align*}
      F_b &= F_{b-1} + \eta f_b, \\
      w_j^\ast &= -\frac{\sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal R_j}\bigl(F_{b-1}(\bm x_{t',i'}) - \tilde y_{t',i'}\bigr)}
        {n_j + \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}}} .
    \end{align*}
    At round $b$, tree $f_b$ is grown to minimize the regularized second-order objective
    \[
      \sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal W_{t,i}} \Bigl[\bigl(F_{b-1}(\bm x_{t',i'}) - \tilde y_{t',i'}\bigr)
        f_b(\bm x_{t',i'})
        + \tfrac12 f_b(\bm x_{t',i'})^2\Bigr]
      + \gamma^{\mathrm{tree}} J + \lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}} \lVert \bm w \rVert_1
      + \tfrac12 \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}} \lVert \bm w \rVert_2^2 ,
    \]
    where $\gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}$ penalizes tree complexity per leaf and $\lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}}, \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}}$ apply $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ shrinkage to the leaf weights $\bm w$.
  \item Every leaf is required to contain at least $n_{\min}$ observations ($n_j \ge n_{\min}$), which corresponds to the minimum leaf size in LightGBM and, under unit Hessian for squared-error loss, the minimum child weight in XGBoost.

\item \textbf{Evaluation set.} Because every forecast is generated by a model estimated on a strictly trailing window, all predictions are out of sample. \item \textbf{Primary loss criterion.} Our primary statistical loss is the daily quasi-likelihood (QLIKE) loss of \citet{Patton2011}, which is robust to measurement noise in the realized-variance proxy.
  % 2026-10-16 (user): parked -- Related work no longer surveys forecast evaluation. The cite stays on this loss.
  % Was: "... proxy (Section~\ref{sec:rh_related})."
  Because the diurnal factor $s^2_{t,c}$ cancels between $\RV_t = y_t^2 s^2_{t,c}$ (with unwinsorized $y_t$) and $\hat\sigma^2_t = \hat y_t^{\,2} s^2_{t,c}$, the daily loss takes the form
  \[
    L_t = \frac{y_t^2}{\hat y_t^{\,2}} - \log\frac{y_t^2}{\hat y_t^{\,2}} - 1
      = \QLIKE\bigl(\RV_t,\, \hat\sigma^2_t\bigr),
  \]
  with sample average over $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ given by
  \[
  \overline{\QLIKE} = \bar L = \frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{oos}}}\sum_{t \in \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}} L_t .
  \]

\item \textbf{Out-of-sample $R^2$.} Following \citet{CampbellThompson2008}, we compute $R^2_{\mathrm{OOS}}$ relative to the expanding historical mean of closing-interval realized variance known at the forecast origin:

\item \textbf{Entry prices.} From the legs' bid quotes $b$ and ask quotes $a$ at 15:30 ET, we define the package mid-quote $P_t$, bid $P^{b}_t$, and ask $P^{a}_t$ as
  \[
  P_t = \tfrac12\bigl(b^C_t + a^C_t\bigr) + \tfrac12\bigl(b^P_t + a^P_t\bigr),
  \qquad
  P^{b}_t = b^C_t + b^P_t, \qquad P^{a}_t = a^C_t + a^P_t .
  \]
% 2026-10-17 (user, E18): parked -- the close named as the official S\&P 500 close. Was: Settlement in cash at the official close $S^{\mathrm{close}}_t$, ...
\item \textbf{Settlement.} The package settles in cash at the official S\&P~500 close $S^{\mathrm{close}}_t$ with no intraday delta hedging; the simple return on the mid-quote premium paid at entry is
  \[
  X_t = \bigl(S^{\mathrm{close}}_t - K_C\bigr)^+ + \bigl(K_P - S^{\mathrm{close}}_t\bigr)^+,
  \qquad
  R_t = \frac{X_t}{P_t} - 1 \;\ge\; -1 .
  \]
% Code: atm_straddle_lib.py:1725-1741 (settle_package); R = exit / entry - 1 (notebooks/_write_0dte_nb.py:452).
\item \textbf{Implied variance.} Let $\mathrm{IV}^C_t$ and $\mathrm{IV}^P_t$ denote the call and put implied volatilities at 15:30 ET, quoted on a per-hour basis. The implied volatility over the closing half hour is
  \[
  \mathrm{IV}_t = \frac{\mathrm{IV}^C_t + \mathrm{IV}^P_t}{2\sqrt2},
  \]
  and $\mathrm{IV}_t^2$ is the corresponding implied variance to expiration.
% Code: atm_straddle_lib.py:1450-1464 (mean of the two legs, / sqrt 2; NaN if either leg is a censored solver node);
% methods_close_option.tex:540-546.
\item \textbf{Forecast variance risk premium.} Following \citet{CarrWu2009} and \citet{BollerslevTauchenZhou2009}, the variance risk premium over the closing half hour is $\mathrm{IV}_t^2 - \E_t[\RV_t]$, which we forecast by $\mathrm{IV}_t^2 - \hat\sigma^2_t$, where $\hat\sigma^2_t$ is the model variance forecast from Section~\ref{sec:rh_methods_setup}. Every trading rule below conditions on the forecast exclusively through the variance gap $\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2$, taking a long straddle position when forecast variance exceeds implied variance.

\item \textbf{Trading strategies.} A strategy chooses a daily straddle position $q_t$ ($q_t > 0$ long, $q_t < 0$ short) and earns the daily return $r_t = q_t R_t$. Because the variance forecast enters solely through $q_t$, comparing performance across rules isolates the economic value of the forecast \citep{FlemingKirbyOstdiek2001}.

We consider four rules:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Unconditional short-straddle benchmark:} a static short-variance position setting $q_t \equiv -1$;
  \item \emph{Sign strategy:} $q_t = \sign\bigl(\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2\bigr)$, with ties mapped to $q_t = -1$;
  % 2026-10-15 (consolidation): dummy day index u -> t' in the three rules below (u is an exogenous series).

  % $m_t = \operatorname{median}_{t'<t}|\hat\sigma^2_{t'} - \mathrm{IV}_{t'}^2|$; full long, scaled short:
  % $q_t = \max((\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2)/m_t, -1)$.
  \item \emph{Robust clip:} $q_t = \clip\bigl((\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2)/\mathrm{MAD}_t, -1, 1\bigr)$, where $\mathrm{MAD}_t = \operatorname{median}_{t'<t}\bigl|\hat\sigma^2_{t'} - \mathrm{IV}_{t'}^2\bigr|$ is the expanding median absolute variance gap over earlier days $t' < t$ in $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$;
  % 2026-10-18 (user, second-list N11): parked -- the full long, scaled short rule: no result for the pooled intraday forecasts is reported (the model-set macro \rheSzLfssMed stays in the generator, unused). Was:

  \item \emph{Percentile rank:} the sign of the gap scaled by the empirical percentile rank of its magnitude across the $t - 1$ preceding days $t' < t$ in $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}$:
    \[
    q_t = \sign\bigl(\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2\bigr)\cdot\frac{1}{t-1}\sum_{t'<t}
      \mathbf{1}\bigl\{|\hat\sigma^2_{t'} - \mathrm{IV}_{t'}^2| \le |\hat\sigma^2_t - \mathrm{IV}_t^2|\bigr\}.
    \]
  \end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Execution.} At mid-quotes, the strategy return is $r_t = q_t R_t$. At quoted bid and ask prices, buying the straddle pays the ask $P^{a}_t$ and selling receives the bid $P^{b}_t$; because settlement occurs in cash at expiration, the bid--ask spread is incurred at entry only:

\begin{tablenotes}[flushleft]
\footnotesize
\item \textit{Notes:} Rolling forecasts from \rhoosSpanStart{} to \rhoosSpanEnd{}, every forecast made with a model estimated on its trailing window only, so every forecast is out of sample; each is scored against the actual realized variance of the closing half hour, $\RV_t$, on the $T_{\mathrm{oos}} = \rhoosDays$ trading days on which every forecast of both training schemes exists, early closes dropped (Section~\ref{sec:rh_results_eval}). The span starts with the intraday linear forecasts, on the first trading day after the pre-sample on which the penalties were selected (\cmPtValFirst{} to \cmPtValLast). The MSE entries are in units of $10^{-\rhoosMseExp}$: the printed number times $10^{-\rhoosMseExp}$ is the mean squared error $T_{\mathrm{oos}}^{-1}\sum_t (\RV_t - \hat\sigma^2_t)^2$. QLIKE is the mean QLIKE loss. $R^2_{\mathrm{OOS}} = 1 - \sum_t (\RV_t - \hat\sigma^2_t)^2 / \sum_t (\RV_t - \overline{\RV}_{t-1})^2$, in percent, where the benchmark $\overline{\RV}_{t-1}$ is the historical mean of the closing-half-hour realized variance over all trading days from \rhoosBenchStart{} to day $t-1$ \citep{CampbellThompson2008}. All features is the full predictor set of Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}; the OLS is estimated on the HAR benchmark only (--: no forecast). Each model is estimated on the last 30 minutes of each trading day only (one observation per day); the OLS on the HAR benchmark is the benchmark forecast. Trees use fixed hyperparameters and are re-estimated daily (Section~\ref{sec:rh_exp_schemes}). The intraday models on the same days are in Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}.
\end{tablenotes}
\end{threeparttable}
\end{table}

\section{Statistical tests}
\label{sec:rh_methods_tests}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Diebold--Mariano test.} To compare the predictive accuracy of two competing forecasts $A$ and $B$, we apply the \citet{DieboldMariano1995} test to the daily QLIKE loss differentials, incorporating the small-sample adjustment of \citet{HarveyLeybourneNewbold1997} for one-step-ahead forecasts:
  \[
    d_t = L_t^{A} - L_t^{B}, \qquad
    \DM = \sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal O| - 1}{|\mathcal O|}}\;
      \frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\hat\Omega / |\mathcal O|}} .
  \]
  % 2026-10-15 (finish): parked -- the horizon symbol h (also the boosting Hessian h_{t'}) dropped; every forecast
  % is one step ahead, so h = 1 is substituted: (|O| + 1 - 2h + h(h-1)/|O|)/|O| = (|O| - 1)/|O|. Was:
  % \DM = \sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal O| + 1 - 2h + h(h-1)/|\mathcal O|}{|\mathcal O|}}\;
  %   \frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\hat\Omega / |\mathcal O|}}, \qquad h = 1 .
  % 2026-10-15 (notation pass): parked -- the uncorrected and corrected statistics merged into one symbol, \DM
  % (the HLN-corrected one, as the code reports); n scored days -> |O|. Old display:
  % \mathrm{DM} = \frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\hat\Omega / n}}, \qquad
  % \mathrm{DM}^{\ast} = \mathrm{DM} \sqrt{\frac{n + 1 - 2h + h(h-1)/n}{n}}, \qquad h = 1 .
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Here $A$ and $B$ denote competing forecast series $f_{m,\mathcal X,\mathcal I}$, indexed by the model class $m$, the predictor set $\mathcal X \in \{\mathrm{HAR}, \mathrm{Full}\}$, and the estimation interval set $\mathcal I \in \{\{c\}, \{1, \dots, M\}\}$.
  % 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- "out-of-sample days"; the evaluation set and the option-data subsample. Was:
  % "\item $\mathcal O$: the out-of-sample days of the exercise, numbered $t = 1, \dots, |\mathcal O|$ in time order;
  %   $\mathcal O = \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$, $|\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}| = T_{\mathrm{oos}}$, in the headline
  %   comparison."
  \item The evaluation set $\mathcal O$, indexed chronologically by $t = 1, \dots, |\mathcal O|$, equals the full evaluation span $\mathcal O = \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ ($|\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}| = T_{\mathrm{oos}}$) for statistical accuracy comparisons and the option-data subsample $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}} \subset \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ for straddle return comparisons (Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}).
  \item We denote by $\bar d$ the sample mean of $d_t$ over $\mathcal O$ and compute two-sided $p$-values under the standard normal distribution as $p = 2\bigl\{1 - \Phi(|\DM|)\bigr\}$.
  \item Under this sign convention, $\DM < 0$ indicates that forecast $A$ achieves a lower average loss than forecast $B$. Throughout the paper, ``statistically significant'' refers to significance at the 5\% level ($p < 0.05$).
  % 2026-10-15 (user): merged from Forecast evaluation (moved from 06_results.tex): the p-value formula, the sign
  % convention and the meaning of "significant". Was: "\item $\bar d$: mean loss differential over $\mathcal O$;
  % two-sided $p$-value from the standard normal."

  % \item $\bar d$: mean loss differential over $\mathcal O$; $h$: forecast horizon; two-sided $p$-value from the
  %   standard normal.
  \end{itemize}

    \qquad
    \hat\gamma_j = \frac{1}{|\mathcal O|} \sum_{t=j+1}^{|\mathcal O|} (d_t - \bar d)(d_{t-j} - \bar d).
  \]

  \begin{itemize}

  % i.e. divides by |O| - k, not |O|; newey_west_t (the return test below) divides by |O|, as displayed.

  % 2026-10-18 (user, E13): FLAG (4) resolved -- dm_test now divides gamma_j by |O| (src/evaluation/diebold_mariano.py:67-68), matching this display.

  % line). Was:

  %   $t = \bar r / \sqrt{\hat\Omega_r / |\mathcal O|}$, with $\hat\Omega_r$ the Newey--West variance above computed on a
  %   daily return series $r_t$ in place of $d_t$: a single strategy's return (a test of its mean return) or the difference

\item \textbf{Test of a mean daily return.} For any daily return series $r_t$---either the return of an individual trading strategy or the return differential $\Delta_t$ between two strategies---observed on the $T = \rheSzDays$ post-warmup days $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{+}$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}), we test whether its mean is zero with the procedure that \citet{LazarusLewisStockWatson2018} recommend for the Newey--West estimator:
  \[
    t = \frac{\bar r}{\sqrt{\hat\Omega_r / T}},
    \qquad
    \hat\Omega_r = \sum_{|j| < S} \Bigl(1 - \frac{|j|}{S}\Bigr) \hat\gamma_j,
    \qquad
    \hat\gamma_j = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=|j|+1}^{T} (r_t - \bar r)(r_{t-|j|} - \bar r),
  \]
  with the Bartlett kernel, bandwidth $S = \lceil 1.3\, T^{1/2} \rceil = \rheHACS$, and fixed-$b$ critical values for $b = S/T$ \citep{KieferVogelsang2005}.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The autocovariances divide by $T$, with no small-sample factor; at lag truncation $S - 1$ the estimator equals the Newey--West variance of the previous item.
  \item This bandwidth is larger than that of conventional rules such as $0.75\, T^{1/3}$, which \citet{LazarusLewisStockWatson2018} obtain from the formula of \citet{Andrews1991} for a first-order autoregression with coefficient $0.25$. Combined with fixed-$b$ critical values, it reduces the size distortion of the test when the returns are serially correlated \citep{LazarusLewisStockWatson2018}.
  \item Under the null hypothesis and fixed $b$, the limiting distribution of $t$ is a functional of Brownian motion that depends only on the kernel and on $b$ \citep{KieferVogelsang2005}. We obtain its quantiles by simulation, computing the same statistic on 1{,}000{,}000 independent series of 1{,}000 i.i.d.\ standard normal draws with bandwidth $1{,}000\,b$. This gives the two-sided 5\% critical value \rheHACCV{} and the $p$-values reported in the text, in place of the standard normal value 1.96.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-22 (user, D6): parked -- the Ledoit--Wolf test as the test of every Sharpe statement; it tests the ratio of the pooled daily returns, while the paper's $\SR$ (note D6) averages calendar years, each annualized by its own $A_y$. The Ledoit--Wolf item below is kept as a robustness check. Was: "\item \textbf{Test of equal Sharpe ratios.} A test of $\bar\Delta = 0$ concerns the mean return differential, not the difference between two Sharpe ratios, which divides each strategy's mean return by its own standard deviation. For every statement about a Sharpe ratio difference we therefore use the studentized circular block bootstrap test of \citet{LedoitWolf2008}."
\item \textbf{Test of equal Sharpe ratios.} A test of $\bar\Delta = 0$ concerns the mean return differential, not the difference between two Sharpe ratios, which divides each strategy's mean return by its own standard deviation. For every statement about a Sharpe ratio difference $\Delta\SR = \SR(r^A) - \SR(r^B)$, with $\SR$ the ratio of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}, we therefore use a paired circular block bootstrap of $\Delta\SR$.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Each of \rheBootN{} bootstrap samples joins blocks of \rheBootBlock{} consecutive days, drawn with replacement from the $T$ post-warmup days arranged on a circle; both strategies are resampled on the same days. Each drawn day keeps its own calendar year, and $A_y$ stays at its value in the original sample, so each sample gives $\Delta\SR^{*}$ computed exactly as $\Delta\SR$.
  \item The $p$-value is two-sided, the share of samples with $|\Delta\SR^{*} - \Delta\SR| \ge |\Delta\SR|$. The block length is fixed rather than calibrated, and the random seed is fixed.
  \item The bootstrap is not studentized: $\SR$ averages ratios over calendar years, and no closed-form standard error of that average is used.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Test of equal Sharpe ratios of the pooled daily returns} (robustness). The studentized circular block bootstrap test of \citet{LedoitWolf2008} tests the equality of the Sharpe ratios of the daily returns pooled over the $T$ days, the ratio of the mean to the standard deviation of all $T$ returns. It is the test of the second alternative definition in Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_sharpe_defs} and is reported beside the bootstrap test above in Table~\ref{tab:rh_app_hac_robust}.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item With $u = \bigl(\mu_A, \mu_B, \mathrm E[(r^A_t)^2], \mathrm E[(r^B_t)^2]\bigr)$, the difference of the Sharpe ratios of the daily returns, $\mu_A/\sigma_A - \mu_B/\sigma_B$, is a smooth function $f(u)$; its standard error follows from the delta method and the long-run covariance matrix $\Psi$ of $\bigl(r^A_t, r^B_t, (r^A_t)^2, (r^B_t)^2\bigr)$.
  \item The test statistic is $d = |f(\hat u)| / \mathrm{se}(\hat u)$. Each of \rheLWBoot{} bootstrap samples joins blocks of \rheLWBlock{} consecutive days, drawn with replacement from the $T$ post-warmup days arranged on a circle, and gives $d^{*} = |f(\hat u^{*}) - f(\hat u)| / \mathrm{se}(\hat u^{*})$, with $\Psi$ estimated in that sample by the block-based estimator of \citet{LedoitWolf2008}. The $p$-value is $\bigl(\#\{d^{*} \ge d\} + 1\bigr)/(\rheLWBoot + 1)$.
  \item In the original sample, $\Psi$ is estimated with the Bartlett kernel at bandwidth equal to the block length, whose expectation is approximately that of the block-based estimator; \citet{LedoitWolf2008} use a prewhitened quadratic-spectral kernel at this step. The block length is fixed at \rheLWBlock{} days rather than calibrated; the next item reports the number of rejections at block lengths \rheLWBlockLo{} and \rheLWBlockHi{}. The random seed is fixed.
  \item The test concerns the Sharpe ratios of daily returns over the $T$ post-warmup days, without the year-by-year annualization of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-22 (user, D6): parked -- the Ledoit--Wolf test as the test of the text's Sharpe statements; now the bootstrap of $\Delta\SR$, with the Ledoit--Wolf $p$ beside it. Was: "... the fixed-$b$ test above; and the $p$-value of the \citet{LedoitWolf2008} test. Statements in the text about mean returns use the fixed-$b$ test, and statements about Sharpe ratios use the \citet{LedoitWolf2008} test." and "\item Of the \rhrRobNPairs{} tests of equal Sharpe ratios, \rhrRobLWSig{} reject at the 5\% level with block length \rheLWBlock{}, \rhrRobLWSigLo{} with block length \rheLWBlockLo{} and \rhrRobLWSigHi{} with block length \rheLWBlockHi{}."
\item \textbf{Robustness to the long-run variance estimator.} Table~\ref{tab:rh_app_hac_robust} lists every comparison of strategy returns whose statistical significance Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ} or Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_econ_last30} states.
